report_name: LiteLLM supply chain attack exposes secrets from over 2,400 companies

threat_actors.name: TeamPCP
threat_actors.description: A threat actor group that orchestrated a multi-stage supply chain attack against the LiteLLM project. They compromised the Trivy scanner's CI/CD pipeline to steal PyPI publishing tokens and then published malicious LiteLLM versions containing the SANDCLOCK Stealer.

attack_patterns.name: Trusted Relationship
attack_patterns.description: The attackers abused the trusted relationship between the LiteLLM project and its CI/CD dependency, Trivy. A compromised version of Trivy was used within LiteLLM's trusted build environment to steal PyPI publishing tokens.

attack_patterns.name: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
attack_patterns.description: TeamPCP published malicious versions (1.82.7 and 1.82.8) of the LiteLLM package to the official PyPI repository, compromising the software supply chain for any downstream project that installed these versions.

attack_patterns.name: Unsecured Credentials
attack_patterns.description: The SANDCLOCK Stealer was designed to find and exfiltrate a wide range of unsecured credentials from compromised developer and CI/CD environments, including SSH keys, cloud credentials, and API keys.

attack_patterns.name: Event Triggered Execution
attack_patterns.description: The malicious LiteLLM packages used a Python startup hook (`.pth` file) to automatically execute the SANDCLOCK Stealer whenever the Python interpreter was started on a compromised system, ensuring payload execution for persistence.

malware.name: SANDCLOCK Stealer
malware.description: A credential-stealing payload delivered via malicious LiteLLM packages (versions 1.82.7, 1.82.8). It was designed to harvest SSH keys, cloud credentials (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure), Kubernetes tokens, and AI service API keys from developer and CI/CD environments.

tools.name: LiteLLM
tools.description: A popular open-source AI proxy tool whose PyPI packages were compromised. Malicious versions (1.82.7, 1.82.8) were published to deliver the SANDCLOCK Stealer.

tools.name: Trivy
tools.description: A widely used open-source vulnerability scanner whose CI/CD pipeline was compromised by TeamPCP. The malicious version was used to steal PyPI publishing tokens for the LiteLLM project.

identities.name: 2,488 corporate domains
identities.description: A class of over 2,400 companies whose secrets were exposed in a 153GB data dump resulting from the LiteLLM supply chain attack. The data was harvested from their developer and CI/CD environments.

infrastructure.name: PyPI Repository
infrastructure.description: The official Python Package Index (PyPI) was used by the attackers to host and distribute the malicious versions of the LiteLLM package (1.82.7 and 1.82.8).

indicators.name: Malicious LiteLLM Package Installation
indicators.x_netsecio_sigma_rule:
title: Malicious LiteLLM Package Installation
id: 9c5b1a3d-4e6f-4b8a-8c1d-9e0f1a2b3c4d
status: experimental
description: Detects the installation of specific malicious versions of the LiteLLM Python package associated with the SANDCLOCK Stealer supply chain attack.
references:
  - https://www.hackread.com/litellm-breach-2500-companies-434k-ci-cd-pipelines/
author: cyber.netsecops.io
date: 2026-08-14
tags:
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.initial_access
level: critical
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_base:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'install'
      - 'litellm=='
  selection_versions:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '1.82.7'
      - '1.82.8'
  condition: selection_base and selection_versions
indicators.description: Detects the installation of malicious LiteLLM versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 via pip command line.

indicators.name: Suspicious Python Startup Hook (.pth file) Creation
indicators.pattern:
title: Suspicious Python Startup Hook (.pth file) Creation
id: f8a7b6c5-4d3e-4f2a-8b1c-9d0e1f2a3b4c
status: experimental
description: Detects the creation of .pth files in Python's site-packages directory. These files can be used for persistence by executing code on Python interpreter startup, as seen in the LiteLLM supply chain attack.
references:
  - https://www.hackread.com/litellm-breach-2500-companies-434k-ci-cd-pipelines/
author: cyber.netsecops.io
date: 2026-08-14
tags:
  - attack.t1546
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.execution
level: medium
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\site-packages\'
      - '\dist-packages\'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.pth'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\easy_install.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
indicators.description: Detects the creation of suspicious .pth files in Python's site-packages directory, a technique used by the malicious LiteLLM packages for persistence.

relationships.target_name: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools

relationships.source_name: Suspicious Python Startup Hook (.pth file) Creation
